full_judgment: 5. The claim of the petitioners in both cases is that the land in question belonged to the Ainuddin and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate which was created in the year 1864 and 1877. After 1950, when the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into being, the property was taken over by the government and that was challenged in the civil court. The suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs claiming the land of the Waqf Estate. The matter went on appeal to the High Court and, thereafter, to the Supreme Court of Pakistan where the plaintiff's claim was established. Before us, initially the respondents claimed that the Waqf deed itself was a forgery and sought to produce a certified copy of another deed No.30 for the year 1864. However, in due course, the learned Deputy Attorney General having produced a number of original volumes for the year 1864, which were in the keeping of the District Registry, it became clear that deed No.30 dated 22.04.1864 is indeed a Waqf deed written in Persian and appears at pages 63-67 of Volume No.1 of 1864. The deed is contained within the volume which records Wills and the particular deed No.30 is a deed of Wakfnamah dated 22.04.1864 which was registered on 25.04.1864. In our mind there is no longer any doubt as to the authenticity of the said Waqf deed.
